item.title: They expected a shift of 0.4 of a fringe and measured less than a twentieth of i…
item.description: They expected a shift of 0.4 of a fringe and measured less than a twentieth of it. The idea was simple. If the Earth moves through an ether, light travelling along the direction of motion should take longer than light crossing it, and the difference should appear as a shift in the interference fringes when the apparatus is turned ninety degrees. The path was about eleven metres, folded back and forth with mirrors to make the effect larger. It was not there. The displacement was certainly below one twentieth of the predicted 0.4 fringe, and probably below one fortieth. Because the effect grows with the square of the speed, the Earth's motion through the ether came out under one sixth of its orbital speed, and certainly under a quarter. Nothing was found, and the absence is the result: whatever the observer's motion, light behaves the same, and the ether had nowhere left to be. Source: Michelson & Morley, American Journal of Science (1887) · doi.org/10.2475/ajs.s3-34.203.333

item.title: 🦄 The narwhal's spiral tusk is built from two intertwined helices, not one An i…
item.description: 🦄 The narwhal's spiral tusk is built from two intertwined helices, not one An international team used advanced X-ray imaging to study the narwhal's corkscrew-shaped tooth, a structure unlike the curved tusks of elephants and walruses. At three European synchrotron facilities, they found that the tusk's microscopic building blocks form two helices twisting in opposite directions, creating an exceptionally stable composite material. The study was published in Nature Communications. The tusk can reach two meters in length, up to half the animal's body, and keeps growing throughout lives that can span 70 years. The precise purpose of the tusk remains uncertain, though evidence points mainly to mate selection and social interactions. #narwhal #materials #biology @science

item.title: 🗺 The United States as a Civilization map, from real data Karpathy asked Claude…
item.description: 🗺 The United States as a Civilization map, from real data Karpathy asked Claude to populate a strategy map of the US with real data. Opus 5.5 in Claude Code spent seven hours and wrote 45,000 lines. Thirty-one sources, from the Census and NOAA to FAA, FEMA and CDC. Elevation, land cover, GDP, jobs, power plants, ports, airports, universities, freight and disasters, all reconciled onto one 25 km hex grid. The hard part is not the code but folding thirty agencies with different units and geographies into one grid. Then the translation into game language: gold is GDP, districts are a city's industries, citizens are the workforce — one in four San Jose workers in engineering, science or code, against one in fourteen nationally — and wonders follow published rules. Plus 19 lenses, a City View for 524 metros and an Explorer over 3,100+ counties. MIT-licensed code. And the honest detail from Karpathy: Claude decided to skip a few states, so Alaska and Hawaii are missing. Map: usaciv / Andrej Karpathy @science

item.title: 🌊 The glass salp: a species that waited twenty years for a name In Monterey Bay…
item.description: 🌊 The glass salp: a species that waited twenty years for a name In Monterey Bay, between 280 and 2,200 metres down, drifts a transparent barrel that spent two decades turning up in MBARI's records without a name. Larry Madin of Woods Hole and MBARI has now described it in Marine Biodiversity as Vitreosalpa gemini — a new species and a new genus. It is the first salp known to spend its whole life in the twilight and midnight zones: relatives stay near the surface, some migrating to 800 metres but not living there. Its body is watery and slow, its metabolism lower than that of surface kin, and it feeds on detritus and single-celled protozoans rather than on living phytoplankton. The name marks two traits: glassy transparency and twin embryos. The chains of clones towed by a solitary individual — up to twenty have been seen — breed sexually, each producing two offspring at once, a rare trick among salps that may double reproductive output where relatives are scarce. Video: MBARI #ocean @science

item.title: Crystals can repeat with 2-, 3-, 4- or 6-fold symmetry. This alloy came back wit…
item.description: Crystals can repeat with 2-, 3-, 4- or 6-fold symmetry. This alloy came back with five. The rule is geometric. A crystal repeats by translation, and no arrangement of identical units can turn five times and still close up; regular pentagons tile a floor only by leaving gaps. The pattern showed six five-fold, ten three-fold and fifteen two-fold axes, with spots as sharp as any crystal's, and no lattice to index them. The phase was aluminium with 14 atomic per cent manganese, cooled fast enough to trap it, in grains up to two micrometres across. It is metastable and forms from the melt by a first-order transition. The authors' wording is the careful part: orientational order without translational order. What broke was not the measurement but the definition, which now covers any solid with a sharp diffraction pattern. Source: Shechtman, Blech, Gratias & Cahn, Physical Review Letters (1984) · doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.53.1951

item.title: 🔬 Tiny chip generates UV light where bulky sources couldn't A Harvard-led team …
item.description: 🔬 Tiny chip generates UV light where bulky sources couldn't A Harvard-led team has built a microscopic photonic device that produces roughly 120 times more ultraviolet power than previous comparable designs. The trick: instead of pushing UV light through lossy on-chip channels, the device converts red light into UV light inside a thin-film lithium niobate chip, using a process called frequency upconversion. The work, published in Nature Communications, positions lithium niobate as a compact platform for powerful UV sources, with potential uses from smaller quantum computers to ultra-precise atomic clocks. The strongest number: about 120 times more UV power than earlier comparable devices. The team notes there are nonlinear effects in the device they don't fully understand yet. #UVphotonics #LithiumNiobate #QuantumComputing @science

item.title: 🧠 Neuralink has FDA clearance for its decisive N1 trial On 25 November the FDA …
item.description: 🧠 Neuralink has FDA clearance for its decisive N1 trial On 25 November the FDA allowed Neuralink to launch the LINK Pivotal Study — the first pivotal trial of an implantable brain-computer interface in the United States. It tests safety and effectiveness in people with severe paralysis from ALS: the N1 chip, 1,024 electrodes on 64 threads, is placed by the R1 robot, and a decoder turns motor-cortex activity into cursor motion. Behind it are more than thirty participants in the US, Canada and the UK; in earlier reports people reached up to 40 words per minute by thought. The clearance covers a study, not a sale: the implant stays investigational. A January 2026 report notes performance varies between patients, and in the first participant some threads partly retracted from the tissue. Critics, among them Surjo Soekadar of Charité, say the company discloses little about complications and that non-invasive eye tracking would spare some patients a risky operation. Video: Neuralink #BCI @science

item.title: The ring around the black hole in M87 is 42 microarcseconds across, give or take…
item.description: The ring around the black hole in M87 is 42 microarcseconds across, give or take three. That number belongs to the instrument, not to the galaxy: eight radio stations, recording at a wavelength of 1.3 millimetres, combined into a single aperture as wide as the Earth by very long baseline interferometry. The image that came out is an asymmetric bright ring with a dark centre, brighter on one side, with a flux ratio above 10 to 1 between ring and shadow. At the distance of the Moon, 42 microarcseconds would span about eight centimetres. A credit card left on the lunar surface is the smallest thing that eye could resolve. The ring is light from behind the hole, bent around it; the darkness inside is the shadow of the horizon, and the asymmetry is gas orbiting near the speed of light. From the ring's size the collaboration weighed the hole at 6.5 billion Suns. Source: EHT Collaboration, ApJ Letters (2019) · doi.org/10.3847/2041-8213/ab0ec7

item.title: 🐝 Wasps have their own biological Face ID — remarkably similar to ours. Researc…
item.description: 🐝 Wasps have their own biological Face ID — remarkably similar to ours. Researchers have identified specialized neurons in the brains of northern paper wasps that respond to individual facial features of other wasps. Despite having only around a million neurons, these insects use a facial recognition mechanism strikingly similar to that found in primates. It helps them maintain social hierarchies without constantly fighting. The study suggests that evolution independently developed similar neural solutions in insects and mammals, although their mechanisms are not identical. Perhaps intelligence is not just about brain size, but how efficiently neurons are organized. #Science #Neuroscience #Evolution #Biology #Intelligence https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cell.2026.10.052
